label: Python
description: Core Python MCQ: data structures, mutability, scoping, comprehensions, exceptions and iterators for web developers.

questions.title: What is the type of `3 / 2` in Python 3?
questions.prompt: What is the type of `3 / 2` in Python 3?
questions.explanation: Python 3's `/` always returns a float. Floor division `//` returns an int (and a float when an operand is a float).

questions.title: Why is a mutable default argument considered a bug?
questions.prompt: Why is a mutable default argument considered a bug?

content.value:
def add_item(item, items=[]):
    items.append(item)
    return items

add_item("a")
add_item("b")

options.text: The default list is created once at function definition and shared across calls, so it returns `['a', 'b']`
Each call creates a fresh list, so it returns `['b']`
Python raises a `TypeError` for mutable defaults
The list becomes a tuple automatically

questions.explanation: Default values are evaluated once when the `def` executes. Use `items=None` and `items = items if items is not None else []` inside the body.

questions.title: What does `nums[::-1]` return?
questions.prompt: What does `nums[::-1]` return?

options.text: `[3, 2, 1]` and then `[1, 2, 3]` — slicing returns a new list and does not mutate
`[3, 2, 1]` twice, because the slice reversed the original
A `TypeError`, because step cannot be negative

questions.explanation: A step of `-1` walks the sequence backwards and builds a new list. `nums.reverse()` or `nums[:] = nums[::-1]` would mutate in place.

questions.title: Which is the idiomatic way to build a string from parts in modern Python?
questions.prompt: Which is the idiomatic way to build a string from parts in modern Python?

options.text: `" ".join(parts)` or an f-string such as `f"{user} scored {score}"`

questions.explanation: `str.join` is O(n) for many parts (repeated `+` is quadratic in the common case) and f-strings are the readable, evaluated-at-runtime formatting introduced in Python 3.6.

questions.title: What is the safest way to read a config value that may be missing?
questions.prompt: What is the safest way to read a config value that may be missing?
questions.explanation: `dict.get(key, default)` returns the default instead of raising `KeyError`. `pop` removes the entry, and a bare `except:` hides unrelated bugs.

questions.title: What does this print, and why?
questions.prompt: What does this print, and why?

content.value:
total = 0

def add(amount):
    total = total + amount

add(5)

options.text: `UnboundLocalError` — assigning inside the function makes `total` local, so reading it before assignment fails; use `global total` or restructure
`5` — Python resolves names to the enclosing scope at call time

questions.explanation: Any assignment in a function body makes the name local for the whole function unless declared `global`/`nonlocal`, so the right-hand read sees an unbound local.

questions.title: Which comprehension squares only the even numbers?
questions.prompt: Which comprehension squares only the even numbers?

options.text: `[n ** 2 for n in nums if n % 2 == 0]`
`[n ** 2 if n % 2 == 0 for n in nums]`
`{n: n ** 2 for n in nums if n % 2}`

questions.explanation: The trailing `if` filters elements. `B` is invalid syntax (a conditional expression needs an `else`), and `D` builds a dict keyed by odd `n`.

questions.title: What does this handler print?
questions.prompt: What does this handler print?

options.text: `bad number` then `done` — `else` runs only when no exception was raised
Nothing — the exception propagates because `ValueError` is not caught

questions.explanation: `int("12a")` raises `ValueError`, so the `else` block is skipped; `finally` always runs.

questions.title: A generator is consumed twice in a loop-heavy report. What happens on the second pass?
questions.prompt: A generator is consumed twice in a loop-heavy report. What happens on the second pass?

content.value:
def pages():
    yield 1
    yield 2

rows = pages()
print(sum(rows))
print(list(rows))

options.text: The second pass yields nothing — a generator is exhausted after one iteration, so `list(rows)` is `[]`; materialise with `list(pages())` if you need it twice
The generator restarts automatically from the beginning
A `StopIteration` propagates and crashes the program
The second pass re-runs the function body from the first `yield`

questions.explanation: Generators are one-shot iterators: once exhausted they are empty. Call the generator function again or store a list to iterate more than once.

questions.title: Why can a `dict` key be a tuple but not a list?
questions.prompt: Why can a `dict` key be a tuple but not a list?

options.text: Dict keys must be hashable; a list's hash would change when its contents change, so only immutable types such as tuples can be keys
Lists are too large to store as keys
Tuples are sorted internally, lists are not
A tuple is copied on assignment, a list is not

questions.explanation: Hashing relies on the value staying stable. Mutable containers do not define `__hash__`, so `d[[1, 2]] = "x"` raises `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'`. A tuple of immutables is hashable (a tuple containing a list is not).

questions.title: Which object is immutable?
questions.prompt: Which object is immutable?
questions.explanation: Tuples, strings, bytes and numbers are immutable; lists, dicts and sets can change after creation.

questions.title: What does `letters[1:4]` return?
questions.prompt: What does `letters[1:4]` return?
questions.explanation: Slices are half-open: the start is included and the stop excluded, so [1:4] takes indexes 1, 2 and 3.

questions.title: What is the last index of a list of five items?
questions.prompt: What is the last index of a list of five items?
questions.explanation: Python uses zero-based indexing, so a length-5 list runs 0..4; `list[-1]` also references the last item.

questions.title: What does `"hi".upper()` return?
questions.prompt: What does `"hi".upper()` return?
questions.explanation: String methods never mutate — they return a new string, so the return value must be used.

questions.title: Where does a module-level variable live?
questions.prompt: Where does a module-level variable live?
questions.explanation: Module-level names live in the global namespace; functions read from it before falling back to builtins.

questions.title: How do you read a dictionary value without raising KeyError?
questions.prompt: How do you read a dictionary value without raising KeyError?
questions.explanation: `get` returns the optional default when the key is missing; `[]` raises KeyError instead.

questions.title: Which keyword catches an exception?
questions.prompt: Which keyword catches an exception?
questions.explanation: `try: … except E: …` (optionally `as e`) handles errors; Python has no catch or rescue keyword.

questions.title: What does `[n*n for n in range(4)]` produce?
questions.prompt: What does `[n*n for n in range(4)]` produce?
questions.explanation: range(4) yields 0..3 and the comprehension squares each value — 0, 1, 4, 9.

questions.title: What does `iter([1,2,3])` return?
questions.prompt: What does `iter([1,2,3])` return?

options.text: An iterator that yields each element once

questions.explanation: iter() wraps the sequence in an iterator; next() then yields one item per call until StopIteration.

questions.title: What does `a = b[:]` do versus `a = b`?
questions.prompt: What does `a = b[:]` do versus `a = b`?

options.text: It makes a shallow copy — mutating a leaves b alone, but nested objects are shared

questions.explanation: Slicing copies the container only; elements inside are referenced, so nested mutable objects remain shared.

questions.title: Why is a mutable default argument a classic bug?
questions.prompt: Why is a mutable default argument a classic bug?

options.text: The default object is created once at definition time and shared by every call

questions.explanation: Append to a default list and the change persists for later calls. The fix is `arg=None`, creating the object inside the function.

questions.title: What does `is` compare that `==` does not?
questions.prompt: What does `is` compare that `==` does not?

options.text: Object identity — whether both names point at the same object

questions.explanation: `==` compares values; `is` compares identity. Two equal strings built separately can compare equal without being the same object.

questions.title: How does `dict.keys()` differ from `list(d)`?
questions.prompt: How does `dict.keys()` differ from `list(d)`?

options.text: keys() is a live view supporting set operations; list(d) snapshots the keys

questions.explanation: Views stay in sync with the dict and support |, & and -; the list is a fixed snapshot taken at that moment.

questions.title: When is `nonlocal` required in a nested function?
questions.prompt: When is `nonlocal` required in a nested function?

options.text: To rebind a name in an enclosing function's scope instead of creating a local one

questions.explanation: `global` targets the module scope while `nonlocal` targets the nearest enclosing function — both must precede an assignment.

questions.title: In `try / except / else / finally`, when does `else` run?
questions.prompt: In `try / except / else / finally`, when does `else` run?

options.text: Only when no exception was raised
Only when an exception was caught

questions.explanation: else runs when the try body completed cleanly; finally runs unconditionally, last, before control leaves the construct.

questions.title: What is the result of `{k: v for k, v in pairs if v}`?
questions.prompt: What is the result of `{k: v for k, v in pairs if v}`?

options.text: A dict keeping only truthy values

questions.explanation: `key: value` makes it a dict comprehension and the trailing `if` filters out falsy values.

questions.title: What does the f-string format spec `{value:>10.3f}` produce?
questions.prompt: What does the f-string format spec `{value:>10.3f}` produce?

options.text: The value right-aligned in a 10-wide field with exactly 3 decimals

questions.explanation: `>` aligns right, `10` is the width, `.3f` fixed-point with precision 3 — the usual table formatting.

questions.title: What is the main benefit of a generator function?
questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of a generator function?

options.text: It runs faster in all cases
It yields values lazily, so only one item is held in memory at a time

questions.explanation: Generators keep only their frame state, so even a very large (or infinite) sequence can be consumed in constant memory.

questions.title: What does `sorted(xs, key=len, reverse=True)` return?
questions.prompt: What does `sorted(xs, key=len, reverse=True)` return?

options.text: xs sorted in place, longest last
A new list sorted by length, longest first, with xs unchanged

questions.explanation: sorted() never mutates its input; key supplies the comparison and reverse=True flips ascending to descending.

questions.title: What does `dict.fromkeys(["a","b"], 0)` share between the two entries?
questions.prompt: What does `dict.fromkeys(["a","b"], 0)` share between the two entries?

options.text: Only the integer 0 (immutable, so it is harmless)

questions.explanation: fromkeys assigns the *same* value object to every key — harmless for ints/strings, but `fromkeys(keys, [])` would share one list across all keys.

questions.title: What is the LEGB rule for name resolution?
questions.prompt: What is the LEGB rule for name resolution?

options.text: Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in — in that order

questions.explanation: Python looks up a bare name in Local → Enclosing → Global → Built-in scopes, stopping at the first match.

questions.title: What does `yield from sub_gen()` do?
questions.prompt: What does `yield from sub_gen()` do?

options.text: Delegates to the sub-generator, yielding its values and passing send/throw through — flattening the chain

questions.explanation: yield from is delegation: it yields every value from the inner generator and forwards send()/throw() directly to it.

questions.title: Why are strings but not lists usable as dict keys?
questions.prompt: Why are strings but not lists usable as dict keys?

options.text: Strings are immutable and hashable; mutable containers have no stable hash

questions.explanation: Keys must be hashable and unchanging, otherwise the bucket they were placed in could silently go stale.

questions.title: What does `except Exception:` fail to catch?
questions.prompt: What does `except Exception:` fail to catch?

options.text: SystemExit, KeyboardInterrupt and GeneratorExit — those derive from BaseException, not Exception

questions.explanation: Catching Exception is idiomatic for application errors, while process-level signals (BaseException) are deliberately allowed to escape.

questions.title: Why is a large list comprehension sometimes replaced with a generator expression?
questions.prompt: Why is a large list comprehension sometimes replaced with a generator expression?

options.text: The generator avoids allocating the entire list, trading index access for constant memory

questions.explanation: Use a generator when you consume values once (sum, any, for-loop); use a list when you need to index, len() or iterate repeatedly.

questions.title: What does `d.setdefault(k, factory_fn())` do that `d.get(k)` does not?
questions.prompt: What does `d.setdefault(k, factory_fn())` do that `d.get(k)` does not?

options.text: It always calls factory_fn() eagerly, and inserts its result when the key is missing

questions.explanation: setdefault evaluates its default eagerly — passing a value (not a lambda) computes work even when the key exists, a common trap.

questions.title: What is the output of `xs[::-1]`?
questions.prompt: What is the output of `xs[::-1]`?

options.text: The same list reversed in place
A new list that is the reverse of xs, leaving xs untouched

questions.explanation: A negative step copies and reverses; because it is a slice it returns a new list — xs itself is unchanged.

questions.title: In a module, why does an assignment inside a function make a name local even if a global exists?
questions.prompt: In a module, why does an assignment inside a function make a name local even if a global exists?

options.text: Python decides scope at compile time — any assignment to a name in a function makes it local for the whole function, shadowing the global

questions.explanation: The compiler classifies the name as local on first assignment, so reading before it raises UnboundLocalError — the classic local-variable trap.

questions.title: Why does `"".join(chunks)` beat `total += chunk` when concatenating many strings?
questions.prompt: Why does `"".join(chunks)` beat `total += chunk` when concatenating many strings?

options.text: Strings are immutable, so each += reallocates and copies; join pre-sizes once and copies in a single pass

questions.explanation: Repeated += is O(n²) due to reallocation; str.join performs one allocation — the standard performance idiom for building strings.
